RETROFLAG NesPi 4: Built for Retro Gaming Nostalgia

The RETROFLAG NesPi 4 is unmistakably designed to evoke the original Nintendo Entertainment System. From the front-loading cartridge flap to the grey-and-black color scheme with red accent lines, this case is a love letter to 1980s gaming. But it's not just a pretty shell — the NesPi 4 packs genuinely useful features.

The standout hardware feature is the built-in 2.5" SATA SSD bay hidden under the top cover. A USB 3.0 bridge adapter connects your SSD directly, giving you fast, reliable storage for ROM libraries, media servers, or any project that outgrows a microSD card. The case includes a 40mm cooling fan that keeps temperatures in check even during extended gaming sessions, and the front panel power and reset buttons (paired with the downloadable safe-shutdown script) let you power on and off gracefully without corrupting your SD card.

Port access is clever: the side panel mimics an NES cartridge slot, and everything — USB, Ethernet, HDMI, audio — is accessible without opening the case. The front USB ports are extended to the front flap, which also houses a functional LED indicator. Build quality is solid for ABS plastic, and the case has enough weight to stay put on a desk without sliding around.

The main tradeoff is that this case is larger than most Pi enclosures. It's designed to sit horizontally on a shelf or TV stand, not tuck behind a monitor. And unlike the Argon ONE, there's no GPIO passthrough — if you're breadboarding sensors or hats, you'll need to unscrew the case. But for its target audience (retro gaming emulation fans building a Lakka, RetroPie, or Batocera box), those are minor quibbles.

Argon ONE V3: Premium Cooling in a Compact Aluminum Shell

The Argon ONE V3 takes the opposite design philosophy: function over form, executed with premium materials. The entire top and sides are milled aluminum, which acts as a giant passive heatsink. Combined with a temperature-controlled 30mm PWM fan, the Argon ONE delivers some of the best thermal performance you'll find in any Pi case — the Pi 5 can run at full load without ever hitting throttling territory.

A signature Argon feature is the internal PCB that reroutes all ports to the rear. Every HDMI, USB, Ethernet, and power connection exits from one clean back panel — exactly like a mini desktop PC. This makes cable management dramatically cleaner, especially if your Pi sits on a desk or in a server rack. The magnetic GPIO cover slides off in a second when you need access, then snaps back to hide the pins when you don't.

The power button, mounted on the rear, connects via GPIO and supports safe shutdown out of the box with Argon's one-line install script. The case is also physically smaller and lighter than the NesPi 4, making it a better fit for tight spaces or VESA mounts behind a monitor.

The downside? That aluminum shell can reduce Wi-Fi signal strength. If you rely on Wi-Fi rather than Ethernet, you may notice a weaker connection or need to add an external antenna. And unlike the NesPi 4, there's no built-in SSD bay — you'll need an external USB drive for expanded storage. Aesthetically, it's a sleek black brick — functional and clean, but it won't spark conversations like a mini NES on your shelf.

  • Internal USB-C extender can be fiddly to align during assembly

Our Verdict: RETROFLAG NesPi 4 Wins for Retro Gaming Builds

If your Raspberry Pi is destined to be a retro gaming console, media center, or living-room emulation box, the RETROFLAG NesPi 4 is the clear winner. The NES aesthetic is unmatched — it turns a bare circuit board into something that looks like it belongs under your TV. The built-in SSD bay is genuinely useful for storing large ROM libraries, and the front power/reset buttons make it feel like a real console. At ~$26, you're getting a case with features that would cost extra as add-ons elsewhere.

Choose the Argon ONE V3 if you prioritize thermal performance above all else, need the cleanest possible cable routing, or plan to run your Pi as a headless server where looks don't matter. Its aluminum body is the best passive cooler in the business, and the rear-port design makes it ideal for desk setups or server racks. It's also the better choice if you're building around a Pi 5, since the NesPi 4 is designed for Pi 4/3B+.

Bottom line: For most retro gaming enthusiasts, the RETROFLAG NesPi 4 delivers more fun per dollar. For serious cooling and desktop aesthetics, go Argon.
